prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

For Alexander Moysaenko The black heart of the moon’s visible through the trees from here. Where are you? I’m alone on the road with a dead phone. The birds are flapping overhead but there’s not much light to be guided by. If any horizon becomes visible enough to follow. Forget the rain’s smear, the chafe of fabric at the calf. The money ran out. The diners are stuffed and back for more. Each terrible thing I said to the child will get repeated hopefully as a joke. And like language, these gestures, or a certain way of nodding one’s head, it all eases in with less than a breath. Forget the song’s words, the order of the band’s set tonight. The black moon’s heart’s got that sinister bent and I want to get touched at by the snakes. One of the students in my class used to go bear hunting with his two uncles. They played recordings of distressed animals to lure in tentative animals to kill. This practice is illegal in many places. Because it’s so very effective. I split open the apple and hand the good half to a child on the bus nestled in under the arm of her sleeping mother. Love from here is a long way to go. Get on your bike and ride through the lights.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: For, Alexander, Moysaenko

outputs.L1:
**For Alexander Moysaenko**

The black heart of the moon is visible through the trees from here. Where are you? I’m alone on the road with a dead phone. Birds flap overhead, but there isn’t much light to guide me—if any horizon becomes visible enough to follow.

Forget the rain’s smear, the fabric chafing at the calf. The money ran out. The diners are stuffed and back for more. Each terrible thing I said to the child will, hopefully, be repeated as a joke. And, like language, these gestures—a certain way of nodding one’s head—all ease in with less than a breath.

Forget the song’s words, the order of the band’s set tonight. The black moon’s heart has that sinister bent, and I want to be touched at by the snakes.

One of the students in my class used to go bear hunting with his two uncles. They played recordings of distressed animals to lure tentative animals in to be killed. This practice is illegal in many places because it is so very effective.

I split open the apple and hand the good half to a child on the bus, nestled beneath the arm of her sleeping mother. Love from here is a long way to go. Get on your bike and ride through the lights.
outputs.L2:
**For Alexander Moysaenko**

From this spot, through the branches, I can make out the moon’s darkened heart. Where have you gone? I’m standing by myself on the road, my phone lifeless. Birds beat their wings above me, though there is scarcely enough illumination to steer by—unless some horizon sharpens into something I can pursue.

Pay no attention to the rain blurring everything, or to the cloth rubbing raw against my calf. There is no money left. The diners, already full, return to eat again. I hope every dreadful remark I made to the child will be retold as though it were funny. Like speech itself, these motions—a particular tilt of the head, perhaps—settle into us more quietly than breathing.

Disregard the lyrics and the sequence of songs the band will perform tonight. The heart inside the black moon curves toward menace, and I want the snakes to reach out and touch me.

A student who once took my class went hunting for bears with two of his uncles. To draw cautious creatures close enough to shoot, they broadcast the cries of animals in distress. Many places have outlawed this method precisely because it works so well.

I cut an apple apart and give the unspoiled half to a girl on the bus, tucked beneath her sleeping mother’s arm. From where love begins here, the distance is immense. Climb onto your bicycle and pedal through the lights.
outputs.L3:
The speaker finds themselves alone on a dark road, unable to rely on a dead phone for guidance and struggling to determine which way to go beneath an ominous moon. Their uncertainty is intensified by financial hardship and physical discomfort, as well as by guilt over hurtful words spoken in the past. Together, these pressures create a deep sense of unease, making the surrounding darkness feel both literal and emotional.

Against this troubled backdrop, language and meaning move quietly between people. Words, expressions, and subtle gestures spread from one person to another, even though their exact forms and sequences are eventually forgotten. This idea of transmission takes on a darker dimension in the story of a former student’s uncles, who illegally used recordings of distressed animals to lure bears within range and kill them. The method was disturbingly effective, demonstrating how sound can be used not only to communicate but also to manipulate vulnerability.

Yet the passage does not end in despair. Small acts of kindness and perseverance offer a fragile but meaningful counterweight to fear and cruelty. Sharing an apple with a child becomes a simple gesture of care, while continuing to ride onward through the lights suggests endurance despite uncertainty. These moments do not erase the speaker’s hardship, but they provide a distant sense of love and hope—a reason to keep moving forward even when the road remains dark.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a fragmented journey through a landscape shaped as much by memory and emotion as by physical reality. Moonlit roads, shadowed surroundings, and surreal images from the natural world create an atmosphere of uncertainty and estrangement. The speaker appears isolated from others and perhaps from the self, moving through a world in which past violence and unresolved guilt repeatedly intrude upon the present. Rather than unfolding as a clear narrative, the poem advances through broken impressions and unsettling associations, reproducing the disorientation of someone burdened by memories that cannot be fully confronted or escaped.

Within this darkness, love remains present but distant. It may be separated from the speaker by geography, time, emotional damage, or the consequences of earlier actions. This distance makes affection feel both sustaining and painful: it offers the possibility of belonging while emphasizing how far the speaker has drifted from intimacy. The natural imagery reflects this tension. Although the moon and the surrounding landscape can suggest beauty, they also appear strange and threatening, as if the outer world has absorbed the speaker’s fear, loneliness, and remorse.

The poem’s violence is therefore not merely an isolated event or theme. It becomes part of the emotional atmosphere, shaping how the speaker sees the road, the night, and other people. Guilt fractures perception, turning ordinary details into reminders of harm. Yet the poem does not end in complete despair. Its final gesture—the sharing of an apple—introduces a small but meaningful act of care. The apple is simple, physical, and communal: it can be divided, offered, and received. In contrast to the poem’s earlier fragmentation, this act creates a brief moment of reciprocity.

The ending does not erase the violence or resolve the speaker’s guilt. Instead, it suggests that human connection may survive through modest acts of generosity. Against the vast darkness of the journey, sharing food may seem fragile or insufficient, but that fragility gives the gesture its emotional power. The poem ultimately proposes that tenderness does not have to defeat suffering in order to matter. Even amid isolation, disturbing memories, and distant love, a small act of care can open a path toward recognition, companionship, and the possibility of repair.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal free-verse prose poem dedicated to Alexander Moysaenko, weaving together a black moon, a dead phone, birds, rain, regret, bear hunting, an apple shared with a child, and a final image of biking through city lights.
counterfactuals.output:
**For Alexander Moysaenko**

Tonight the black moon hangs over the forest  
like a door burned shut.

My phone is dead in my pocket,  
its small glass heart refusing every name,  
while birds pour from the pines—  
not flying, exactly, but becoming rain,  
each feather a silver sentence  
the sky regrets having written.

We went bear hunting once,  
or dreamed we did:  
you carried no rifle, only a lantern  
filled with the warm breath of horses,  
and I followed the enormous tracks  
until they entered my own shadow.  
There the bear slept, wearing my face,  
and all my old regret moved inside him  
like bees behind a wall.

At dawn, a child appeared beside the river.  
She held out an apple, green and imperfect.  
We divided it with our hands.  
Half for her hunger, half for mine,  
the seeds shining between us  
like tiny black moons  
waiting to be forgiven.

Then the rain lifted its long transparent curtains.  
The birds returned to whatever heaven  
keeps unfinished songs.  
The phone remained dead.  
No one called from the past.

Alexander, evening opened the city  
one window at a time,  
and there we were—  
biking through the lights,  
our wheels turning stars out of puddles,  
our shadows racing ahead of us,  
bright and impossible,  
as if the night had finally remembered  
how to let us go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental contemporary poem about being stranded alone on a dark road, mixing ominous natural imagery with fragmented memories, guilt, violence, tenderness, and longing.
counterfactuals.output:
**MILE 0 / NO SIGNAL**

The road has forgotten  
what roads are for.

Black ribbon, no gift.  
Pines lean inward  
like jurors exchanging breath.

Somewhere, an animal  
makes the sound of a door  
being opened slowly.

I have no map, only  
the blue corpse-light of my phone,  
only 3%,  
only your last message:

*come home*  
*come—*  
*co—*

and then the dark  
eats the sentence.

***

Memory arrives in pieces:

your hand asleep in mine,  
warm bird, small engine—

the kitchen window punched through  
with rain—

my father washing blood  
from a shovel  
(or was it rust?  
or sunset?  
or nothing I was allowed to name?)

A bowl of peaches  
softening on the table.

You saying,  
Don’t leave like this.

Me leaving  
exactly like this.

***

Wind drags its nails  
along the guardrail.

Beyond it, the ditch  
is full of silver weeds,  
each blade rehearsing  
a little knife.

I think of tenderness  
as something violent time does:

how the moon breaks itself  
across every puddle  
just to touch the road,

how your mouth, after anger,  
still found my forehead—

forgive me, forgive me—  
not words,  
but the pressure of lips  
on a locked door.

***

A truck passes.

For one white second  
the world confesses:

dead moths in the gravel,  
my shadow with its hands up,  
a fox at the tree line  
holding fire in its eyes.

Then gone.

Then engine fading  
like someone who has decided  
not to turn back.

***

I was cruel.

There—  
a flare in the throat.

I threw the glass.  
I wanted the wall  
to understand me.

Instead, the wall opened  
a bright, jagged mouth.

Instead, you went quiet  
in the way snow goes quiet  
over a field  
where something has fallen.

I touched your wrist afterward  
as if touch were a bridge,  
as if bridges cannot burn,  
as if sorrow does not learn  
the address of every house.

***

The road continues  
without mercy or witness.

Above me, clouds move  
their enormous furniture.

The stars are gone,  
but I feel them:  
cold nails behind the sky.

I call your name.

It leaves my body  
and becomes weather.

Again.

Your name—

a match struck  
inside a wolf.

Your name—

the one lit window  
in a town I cannot reach.

***

Morning must exist somewhere.

Perhaps it is already touching  
your closed curtains,  
your cup beside the sink,  
the dent my head made  
in the pillow.

Perhaps you are sleeping  
with one hand open.

Perhaps not for me.

Still, I walk.

Each step:  
a small apology  
the earth does not accept.

Each breath:  
smoke without fire.

Behind me, the dark road  
keeps every version  
of what happened.

Ahead—

nothing,

nothing,

then, very far off,

a trembling amber light  
that could be a house,

or a warning,

or you  
standing barefoot in the doorway,

or only the moon  
caught low in the branches,

tender and terrible,

refusing  
to come closer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-paragraph prose poem in an intimate, disorienting voice. Include the recurring image of the moon’s black heart, an anecdote about illegal bear baiting, and end with the command, “Get on your bike and ride through the lights.”
counterfactuals.output: You wake with your hand inside my dream, feeling for a pulse where the moon’s black heart has been ticking all night, slow as a stranger at the door. I tell you about the summer my uncle was arrested for illegal bear baiting—how he left doughnuts and bacon grease in the pines, then swore the dark itself had eaten them, though we saw the bear at dusk, bewildered and huge, wearing a blue plastic bucket around its neck like a broken halo. You laugh, but your face is already another room, and in it the moon’s black heart swings from a wire, turning our shadows into animals that cannot remember the forest. Come closer; I have misplaced your name beneath my tongue. Outside, sirens stitch the rain to the road, every red window opening and closing like a wound, while the moon’s black heart follows us in the puddles, faithful, impossible, hungry for whatever we leave behind. Get on your bike and ride through the lights.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a darkly lyrical poem for Alexander Moysaenko that moves associatively between a nighttime journey, forgotten song lyrics, cruel words spoken to a child, predatory animals, and an unexpected act of kindness on a bus.
counterfactuals.output:
**Night Bus for Alexander Moysaenko**

The road unspools its black ribbon  
under a moon with one blind eye.  
Pines lean close, whispering  
the half-remembered chorus  
of a song we once knew by heart—  
something about leaving,  
something about snow,  
then only the hum of tires  
where the words should be.

A child in the back seat  
holds his breath like a match.

*You ruin everything,*  
someone told him once,  
and the sentence grew teeth,  
made a den beneath his ribs.  
Years later, it still wakes hungry,  
paces there like a wolf  
that has learned his name.

Beyond the glass, foxes flicker  
through the headlight’s brief kingdom.  
An owl drops soundlessly  
into the grass.  
Every beautiful thing, at night,  
seems to be hunting  
or hunted.

The bus smells of wet wool,  
old coins, oranges.  
No one speaks. Even grief  
has missed its stop.

Then the driver brakes  
for a dog trembling in the road—  
thin as a question,  
eyes bright with terror.

A woman rises without a word,  
removes her red scarf,  
steps down into the cold.  
She wraps the animal gently,  
as though returning a lost verse  
to the mouth of the song.

For one moment, Alexander,  
the darkness does not vanish—  
it merely opens.

And through that narrow mercy  
we travel on,  
carrying the child, the wolf,  
the forgotten refrain,  
and the small warm body  
lifted from the road.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a surreal monologue in free verse about distance and love, using abrupt transitions, uncanny syntax, and images of trees, diners, distressed-animal recordings, snakes, a split apple, and a sleeping mother.
counterfactuals.output:
I loved you from the far side of a glass of water,  
where distance kept changing its shoes.

Listen—  
the trees have entered the diner again,  
dragging their wet roots past the pie display.  
One orders coffee.  
One asks for the road  
served open-faced.

I say your name  
and the jukebox fills with snow.

Under the counter, a small machine plays  
recordings of distressed animals:  
a fox becoming a door hinge,  
a calf calling through static,  
some seabird tearing the sky  
with its invisible receipt.

This is not grief.  
Grief has better manners.

Outside, the highway straightens its long black tie.  
Snakes warm themselves on the center line,  
each one a sentence  
the earth refuses to finish.

You are miles away,  
which is a kind of room  
I keep walking into.

Abruptly: an apple on the table, split clean.  
One half remembers the orchard.  
The other half has your teeth in it.  
Between them, the seeds sit darkly,  
little witnesses in polished coats.

My mother sleeps in the next century.  
Her hands rest above the blanket  
as if she has just released two birds  
or forgotten how to fall.  
Do not wake her.  
The moon is explaining everything  
backward into her ear.

I tell the waitress I am waiting for you.  
She pours more night into my cup.  
Her face is a clock with no animal inside.

Then the trees begin leaving—  
not through the door,  
but upward,  
through the roof,  
through weather,  
through the astonished mouths of stars.

Love, I call after them,  
though love is not their name.

Distance, I call,  
and every snake lifts its head.

Somewhere you turn in your sleep.  
Somewhere the apple closes.  
Somewhere my mother opens her eyes  
and they are two diners at dawn,  
empty except for the hum,  
the coffee cooling,  
and a voice from the little machine  
crying out because it is lost—

or because it has found  
what cannot come nearer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
